headline: Dancing to bat calls: how music is changing minds about misunderstood mammals
meta_description: A new album transforms the echolocation calls of eight bat species into electronic dance music, offering a creative way to shift how people perceive these cruc…
summary_short: Musicians have created an album from bat echolocation calls, turning ultrasonic sounds into dance music to help people see bats differently.
body:
Two artists have released an album made entirely from the echolocation calls of bats, transforming the ultrasonic sounds of eight bat species into electronic music. Echo in the Dark, created by Hanna Tuulikki and Tommy Perman, blends translated bat recordings with the human voice, making audible the clicks, buzzes and rhythms that normally exist beyond human hearing. The project began when Hospitalfield arts venue in Arbroath, Scotland commissioned the work in 2022 after running community bat walks during lockdown. Rather than lecturing listeners, the artists hope the music itself will spark curiosity about creatures that, despite their ecological importance, inspire negative feelings in nearly half of UK adults according to a Bat Conservation Trust survey.

Perman was struck by the variety he discovered in the bats' calls. The lesser horseshoe bat produces rippling sounds that evoke dub records, while the Daubenton's bat creates syncopated rhythms reminiscent of jazz drumming. The sounds were collected through recordings the artists made themselves, an open call to the public, and collaboration with the Tayside Bat Group, eventually capturing calls from eight of the UK's eighteen bat species. The project debuted as outdoor "silent bat raves" where audiences danced through headphones while bats flew overhead at dusk.

Now available as a vinyl and digital album released on 28 August through Glasgow independent label KIN-TU, Echo in the Dark represents something more than novelty. Perman sees dance music as a space where people can lose themselves and feel connected to something larger—and hopes that power can nurture curiosity about the natural world rather than fear. If even a handful of listeners find themselves drawn to listen for bats in the night or support conservation efforts, he says, the album will have succeeded.
quick_facts: Album features eight bat species from the UK transformed into electronic music
Nearly half of UK adults hold negative feelings about bats, survey finds
Project began in 2022 at Hospitalfield arts venue in Arbroath, Scotland
Released 28 August on Glasgow independent label KIN-TU
Artists previously created outdoor silent bat raves with headphone dancing
